reference.source: Renal tubulopathy and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function of the apical sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, so the tubule behaves as if chronically exposed to a loop diuretic.
A prototypical antenatal (neonatal) Bartter subtype presenting with marked polyhydramnios and premature delivery.
Hallmark biochemistry is a hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with hyperreninaemic hyperaldosteronism yet normal or low blood pressure.
Prominent hypercalciuria with early nephrocalcinosis is characteristic and helps separate it from Gitelman syndrome.
Overproduction of prostaglandin E2 amplifies the salt wasting, polyuria and failure to thrive, and prostaglandin synthetase inhibition improves symptoms.
Neonates show severe polyuria, salt craving, recurrent dehydration and poor weight gain.
Blood pressure is preserved or low because chronic volume depletion offsets the high aldosterone.
Distinguished from type 2 by the absence of an early transient hyperkalaemic phase.
reference.pathophysiology: Bartter syndrome type 1 arises from biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC12A1, the gene encoding the apical furosemide-sensitive sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter NKCC2 of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. NKCC2 drives the bulk of sodium chloride reabsorption in this segment and generates the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage that powers paracellular reabsorption of calcium and magnesium. When NKCC2 is defective, sodium chloride is lost into the urine, exactly reproducing the pharmacological effect of a loop diuretic; the resulting volume contraction activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, and enhanced distal sodium delivery drives renal potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, producing a hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Loss of the lumen-positive voltage impairs paracellular calcium reabsorption, causing hypercalciuria and predisposing to nephrocalcinosis. Compensatory overproduction of prostaglandin E2 further amplifies renin release, salt wasting and polyuria, which is why prostaglandin synthetase inhibition is therapeutically effective.
additionalDifferentials: Bartter syndrome type 2 (KCNJ1 / ROMK) — antenatal, with early transient neonatal hyperkalaemia
Bartter syndrome type 3 (CLCNKB / ClC-Kb) — classic, later onset with a broader phenotype
Bartter syndrome type 4 (BSND / barttin) — antenatal salt wasting with sensorineural deafness
Transient antenatal Bartter syndrome type 5 (MAGED2, X-linked) — severe polyhydramnios that resolves after birth
Gitelman syndrome (SLC12A3) — hypocalciuria, hypomagnesaemia and later childhood or adult onset
Surreptitious loop diuretic use or chronic vomiting mimicking the biochemistry
Congenital chloride diarrhoea causing metabolic alkalosis and volume depletion
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes with venous blood gas to document hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, both characteristically elevated
Spot urinary electrolytes including chloride and a urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio demonstrating hypercalciuria
Renal tract ultrasound looking for nephrocalcinosis
Antenatal ultrasound surveillance for polyhydramnios, with amniotic fluid chloride assessment where available
Serum magnesium, usually preserved, which helps distinguish from Gitelman syndrome
Molecular genetic testing of SLC12A1, ideally within an inherited tubulopathy gene panel
redFlags: Severe neonatal hypovolaemia and circulatory collapse from combined salt and water loss
Life-threatening hypokalaemia with cardiac arrhythmia or paralytic ileus
Complications of extreme prematurity following polyhydramnios
Progressive nephrocalcinosis with declining kidney function
reference.prognosis: With early and sustained fluid, salt and potassium replacement together with prostaglandin synthetase inhibition, growth and biochemistry can usually be stabilised. Polyuria persists lifelong, and nephrocalcinosis with a gradual decline in renal function may develop over the long term.
pitfalls: Confusing the metabolic alkalosis with pyloric stenosis or surreptitious vomiting
Mislabelling it as Gitelman syndrome, which is instead hypocalciuric, hypomagnesaemic and later in onset
Overlooking prostaglandin-driven symptoms that respond to prostaglandin synthetase inhibition
Attributing polyhydramnios solely to obstetric causes and missing the underlying tubulopathy
references: Consensus guidance on inherited salt-losing tubulopathies
Clinical genetics and inherited disease reference databases
management: Early and sustained sodium chloride, fluid and oral potassium replacement to counter salt and potassium wasting
Prostaglandin synthetase inhibition with indometacin to reduce the prostaglandin-driven polyuria, salt wasting and failure to thrive
Potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone or amiloride to reduce renal potassium loss
Neonatal support for prematurity and recurrent dehydration, with attention to salt craving and feeding
Monitoring of electrolytes, growth and renal function, with renal ultrasound surveillance for nephrocalcinosis
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and testing of at-risk relatives
